title: Hugging Face Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Hugging Face lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Find the different Hugging Face tools
entries.summary: Hugging Face includes a Hub for shared resources and libraries used in local programs. These are related tools with different jobs.

example.code:
Hub: pages for models, datasets and other resources
Datasets library: load and transform data tables
Tokenizers library: turn text into token IDs
Transformers library: work with many model architectures

notes: A library installation does not mean a trained model has been downloaded.

entries.name: Read a model card before use
entries.summary: A model card explains a shared model's intended use, training information, checks and limits. Also read its licence and files before deciding to use it.

example.code:
Check the model page for:
Task and supported languages
Licence and use conditions
Training and evaluation notes
Known limits
Files and code required to load it

notes: Do not enable trust_remote_code just to bypass an error without reviewing the code it allows to run.

entries.name: Make a dataset from a dictionary
entries.summary: A Dataset holds rows with named columns. from_dict creates a dataset from equally sized lists, one list per column.

example.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon glows", "sun shines", "stars twinkle"], "length": [2, 2, 2]})
print(data.num_rows, data.column_names)

notes: Each column must contain the same number of rows.

entries.name: Select rows by position
entries.summary: select makes a dataset containing chosen row positions. Positions begin at zero, and the requested order is preserved.

example.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon", "sun", "stars"]})
small = data.select([2, 0])
print(list(small["text"]))

notes: A row position is not a permanent record ID if the data is reordered.

entries.name: Filter using a condition
entries.summary: filter keeps rows for which a function returns True. The function receives a row and checks the condition you chose.

example.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon", "sun", "stars"]})
long_words = data.filter(lambda row: len(row["text"]) > 3)
print(list(long_words["text"]))

notes: Filtering can change which kinds of examples are represented; review what is dropped.

entries.name: Add a calculated column
entries.summary: map applies a function to rows and returns an updated dataset. Returning a dictionary can add named fields.

example.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon", "sun"]})
with_lengths = data.map(lambda row: {"characters": len(row["text"])})
print(list(with_lengths["characters"]))

notes: A transformation must use the intended meaning; character count and token count are different measures.

entries.name: Split data for later checks
entries.summary: train_test_split divides a dataset into training and test parts. A seed makes this split repeatable for the same data and tool behaviour.

example.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]})
parts = data.train_test_split(test_size=2, seed=7)
print(parts["train"].num_rows, parts["test"].num_rows)

notes: A repeatable split is not automatically a fair split for every task.

entries.name: Build a tiny word tokenizer
entries.summary: A tokenizer turns text into pieces and IDs. WordLevel uses whole pieces from a supplied vocabulary. Whitespace splits this simple sentence into words.

example.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
encoded = tokenizer.encode("moon glows")
print(encoded.tokens, encoded.ids)

notes: This tiny fixed vocabulary is a teaching tool, not the tokenizer used by every real model.

entries.name: Recognise an unknown token
entries.summary: When a piece is missing from this WordLevel vocabulary, the tokenizer uses its unknown marker. It does not invent a new learned word entry.

example.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
encoded = tokenizer.encode("boat glows")
print(encoded.tokens, encoded.ids)

notes: This tokenizer has no lowercase normalizer; moon and Moon are different inputs.

entries.name: Decode IDs into text
entries.summary: Decoding maps known token IDs back to text. Tokenization may not preserve every detail of original spacing, so test exact-text needs carefully.

example.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
print(tokenizer.decode([2, 3]))

notes: Do not assume encode and decode preserve every input byte for all tokenizer settings.

entries.name: Pad a sequence and inspect its mask
entries.summary: Padding adds filler tokens to reach a chosen length. An attention mask marks real tokens with 1 and padding with 0 in this encoding.

example.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
tokenizer.enable_padding(length=4, pad_id=0, pad_token="[PAD]")
encoded = tokenizer.encode("moon glows")
print(encoded.ids, encoded.attention_mask)

notes: Padding does not shorten an overlong sequence; truncation is a separate choice.

entries.name: Save and reload a local tokenizer
entries.summary: A tokenizer can save its settings as a JSON file. Reloading that file restores the local vocabulary and processing rules.

example.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
tokenizer.save("practice-tokenizer.json")
restored = Tokenizer.from_file("practice-tokenizer.json")
print(restored.encode("moon glows").ids)

notes: Use a practice path to avoid replacing a file you need, and inspect unfamiliar files before loading them.
